REASONING:
Step 1 – Frame the project  
- **Objective:** Increase capacity and reliability of Mongolia’s transmission grid to enable renewable energy (PDO).  
- **Scope & Components:** (1) Construction of a 220 kV double‑circuit transmission line (Baganuur‑Choir) and associated substation upgrades (US$45.84 M). (2) Capacity‑building and implementation support (US$1.16 M IBRD + US$0.84 M counterpart).  
- **Delivery model:** Borrower = Mongolia; Implementing agency = Ministry of Energy (MOE). Project Steering Committee (PSC) and a new Project Management Office (PMO) under MOE will manage implementation.  
- **Timeline:** Loan effective 21‑Nov‑2024; implementation expected to start 2025; key disbursements through 2029; overall program closing 31‑May‑2034.  
- **Budget:** Total operation cost US$47.84 M (IBRD loan US$47 M, counterpart US$0.84 M).  
- **Key stakeholders:** MOE, Ministry of Finance, National Power Transmission Grid (NPTG), Energy Regulatory Commission, World Bank, private renewable developers, local communities, women workforce.  
- **External dependencies:** Procurement market (local firms, import‑heavy material supply), limited construction season (winter), climate hazards, political/election cycle, regulatory limits on VRE connections.

Step 2 – Category sweep (candidate risks with supporting text)  

| Category | Candidate risk | Evidence (≤25 words) |
|---|---|---|
| schedule | Winter construction delay | “If it cannot be completed before winter, the Project will have more delays with waiting for the next construction season.” |
| technical | No local manufacturer for 220 kV poles/conductors | “Also there is no local company who can produce metal poles and conductors meeting the standards for 220kV lines.” |
| technical | Bird‑collision / biodiversity impact | “Transmission lines in Mongolia often involve bird collision and other biodiversity issues… Bird management Plan adjusted to avoid birds' habitat.” |
| technical | OHS risks (electrocution, height work, EMF) | “During operation and maintenance phases… OHS risks… can be easily mitigated in a predictable manner by adopting Good International Industry Practice.” |
| financial | Poor budgeting / fund misuse | “Poor budgeting: The project funds not used for the intended purposes.” |
| financial | Imported construction material cost volatility | “Construction sector… relies on imports… pandemic or border closures could have a significant impact… increased costs and delays.” |
| financial | Weak internal controls | “Weak internal controls: There are not any internal controls related financial management policies and procedures established for the project yet.” |
| organizational | PMO not yet established, no finance staff | “PMO is not yet in place and no financial management staff has been appointed.” |
| organizational | Procurement staff lack English/Bank‑procurement experience | “Evaluation Committee members normally do not have knowledge and experience in handling English documents… may cause delays.” |
| stakeholder | Community access restrictions & safety during civil works | “temporary restriction of access to resources by local herders… traffic increase generated by the construction works.” |
| stakeholder | Gender gap limiting female participation | “Women represent 28.8 % of the total workforce… gaps may persist unless concrete actions are undertaken.” |
| political_regulatory | Change of government officials after election | “Potential changes in Government officials involved in project activities due to election cycle in first half year… H.” |
| political_regulatory | Regulator does not allow further VRE connections | “the regulator also does not allow any more connections of VRE to the region.” |
| environmental | Soil erosion, noise, wetland disturbance, archeological risk | “Construction of new transmission lines… adverse environmental impacts… soil erosion… disruption to wetland areas, may damage archeological sites.” |
| environmental | Climate‑hazard exposure (flood, landslide, extreme cold) | “Mongolia is prone to risks from climate hazards such as flooding, wildfires, and landslides… exposure to drought and extreme cold.” |
| external | Supply‑chain disruption for imported materials | “75‑80 % of construction materials are sourced from outside the country… pandemic or border closures could have a significant impact.” |

Step 3 – Evidence filter  
All listed risks are directly quoted from the PAD; none are removed.

Step 4 – Assess & Mitigate  

| ID | Likelihood (1‑5) | Impact (1‑5) | Justification | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R01 | 4 | 3 | Winter is a fixed constraint; missing the narrow building window pushes work a full season. | Schedule early‑season mobilisation, secure winter‑ready equipment, build a time contingency buffer. |
| R02 | 3 | 3 | Absence of local suppliers forces imports, adding lead‑time uncertainty. | Pre‑qualify foreign manufacturers early, include delivery‑time clauses, consider bulk ordering before winter. |
| R03 | 3 | 2 | Bird collisions are known but mitigated by design; residual risk moderate. | Install certified bird diverters, maintain BMP, monitor post‑construction bird activity. |
| R04 | 3 | 3 | Construction/maintenance on high‑voltage lines carries documented OHS hazards. | Comprehensive OHS plan, mandatory safety training, PPE, third‑party safety audits. |
| R05 | 3 | 4 | Weak budgeting can lead to misallocation of US$47 M, high financial loss. | Enforce annual budgets, quarterly variance analysis, PSC approval of major revisions, independent financial monitoring. |
| R06 | 3 | 4 | Import‑heavy material base makes cost overruns likely under global supply shocks. | Negotiate fixed‑price contracts, add price‑escalation caps, identify alternative suppliers, maintain buffer stock. |
| R07 | 2 | 4 | Absence of internal controls creates high‑impact fraud risk despite lower likelihood. | Draft and implement detailed internal control manual (FMM), segregation of duties, regular internal & external audits. |
| R08 | 4 | 3 | PMO absence at start threatens FM set‑up; staff recruitment risk is high. | Accelerate recruitment of qualified finance officer, provide Bank‑led onboarding, use interim external FM advisors. |
| R09 | 3 | 3 | Language and procedural gaps can delay procurement evaluations. | Conduct English‑procurement training, employ bilingual procurement specialists, use Bank‑provided templates. |
| R10 | 3 | 2 | Community access limits are typical for civil works; impact mainly reputational. | Early community engagement, clear traffic‑management plan, compensation where access is curtailed. |
| R11 | 2 | 2 | Gender gap is present but does not directly threaten core deliverables. | Conduct gender gap assessment, set hiring targets, provide leadership training for women. |
| R12 | 3 | 3 | Elections may replace key officials, causing continuity issues. | Develop a hand‑over plan, maintain updated stakeholder register, engage incoming officials promptly. |
| R13 | 3 | 3 | Regulatory block on VRE connections could limit project’s benefit realization. | Ongoing dialogue with ERC, provide technical evidence for capacity, seek amendment to VRE connection rules. |
| R14 | 3 | 2 | Environmental disturbances are temporary and mitigable. | Implement erosion control mats, avoid wetlands where possible, monitor impacts, restore disturbed areas. |
| R15 | 3 | 3 | Climate events can damage towers; design includes resilience but risk remains. | Apply climate‑resilient engineering standards (wind, snow, seismic), conduct regular inspections, emergency response plan. |
| R16 | 2 | 3 | Global supply shocks are possible but less likely in short term. | Diversify supplier base, maintain safety stock, include force‑majeure clauses in contracts. |

Step 5 – Consolidate  
All 16 risks are distinct and directly evidenced; they are retained in the register.
